knownFor: Bishop, preacher and poet whose sermons on the Trinity and letters on Christ's full humanity became standards for the later church.

traces: Gennadius of Marseilles, calling Gregory of Nazianzus that most eloquent man, reports that Rufinus of Aquileia put his works into Latin along with those of Basil of Caesarea.
With Basil of Caesarea he gathered the Philocalia, a book of choice passages from Origen. About Easter in 382 he sent a copy to a friend as a book useful to students of literature.
In 553 the emperor Justinian's letter to the council at Constantinople named Gregory the Theologian among the holy Fathers it followed.

Sozomen, in his chapter on the second general council, which he heads with the abdication of Gregory the Theologian, says Gregory at first consented to lead the church of Constantinople, then withdrew his consent on learning that some of the bishops, particularly those of Egypt, objected. His modern translators Browne and Swallow add that after Meletius of Antioch died, Gregory took the chair of the council.
remembered: Theodoret remembered him among the great teachers of the imperial city, as Gregory of Nazianzus, shining friend and supporter of the truth.

Jerome called him a most eloquent man and his instructor in the Scriptures, and counted thirty thousand lines of his writing. He remembered asking Gregory of Nazianzus about a hard verse, and Gregory teasing that he would explain it in church, where the applause would force Jerome to understand.

uncertain: Whether he ever took up Sasima is unclear. It seems he did not, with a rival bishop's troops holding the village and his father pleading with him to stay. His own letters pull two ways. In one he says he was appointed to Sasima, though for a short time he governed Nazianzus out of respect for his father. In another he says he was originally appointed to Nazianzus, "and not to Sasima as some would falsely persuade you".

When and why he gave up Constantinople is told two ways. Socrates says he resigned when the emperor arrived, because some murmured that he was a stranger. Sozomen says he withdrew at the council, after some bishops, particularly those of Egypt, objected to his election. The brief follows Sozomen.

quotationOriginals.work: Gregory of Nazianzus, Letters 48-50 to Basil, tr. Browne and Swallow

quotationOriginals.modern: as if I were fighting for souls and church canons?
quotationOriginals.printed: as though for souls and canons?
quotationOriginals.work: Gregory of Nazianzus, Letters 48-50 to Basil, tr. Browne and Swallow
quotationOriginals.uncertain: "Canons" may mean church rules or a bishop's canonical rights of jurisdiction, which were at stake in the quarrel. Both readings are kept.

quotationOriginals.uncertain: "Confusion" here means fusing Father, Son and Spirit into one, not bewilderment. "Division" means splitting God into unequal parts.
